title: A Letter to God
subject: English

notes.heading: Word Meanings
points: Crest: The very top part of a mountain or a hill.
Downpour: A very heavy and intense fall of rain.
Intimately: Having deep, detailed, or very close knowledge of something.
Draped: Covered or wrapped loosely with a layer of something.
Hailstones: Small, hard balls of ice that fall from the sky like rain.
Plague of locusts: A massive, destructive swarm of insects that completely ruins crops.
Solitary: Living or existing completely alone or isolated in a place.
Conscience: A person's inner moral sense of what is right and wrong.
Ox of a man: An idiom used to describe a person who is extremely strong and hardworking.
Pesos: The basic unit of currency used in several Latin American countries.
Amiable: Having or displaying a very friendly, warm, and pleasant manner.
Correspondence: The act of communicating with someone by exchanging letters.
Resolution: A firm, unshakeable decision to do something.
Contentment: A state of peaceful happiness and complete satisfaction.
Crooks: Dishonest people, cheats, or criminals.

summary: "A Letter to God" by G.L. Fuentes is a touching story that explores the power of unconditional faith and the bittersweet irony of human nature. The narrative revolves around Lencho, a hardworking farmer whose house sits alone on the crest of a low hill, overlooking his cornfield that promises a great harvest. Lencho eagerly awaits rain, but a much-needed shower suddenly transforms into a devastating hailstorm, accompanied by strong winds that completely ruin his crops, leaving the field looking as white as if covered with salt. With his entire year's labor destroyed and his family facing starvation, Lencho refuses to lose hope because of his deep, unwavering faith in the almighty, believing that no one dies of hunger under the watchful eyes of the creator. Since he knows how to write, he writes a letter addressed directly to God, explaining his desperate situation and requesting one hundred pesos to sow his field again and support his family until the next harvest. He walks to town, places a stamp on the envelope, and drops it into the mailbox. At the post office, a postman finds the unusually addressed letter and bursts out laughing before showing it to the postmaster. The postmaster, a fat and friendly man, is initially amused but quickly turns serious, profoundly moved by Lencho's immense faith. Determined not to shake the writer's trust, he decides to answer the letter by collecting money from his employees, contributing a part of his own salary, and asking his friends for acts of charity. Despite his best efforts, he manages to gather only seventy pesos, which he puts inside an envelope addressed to Lencho, signing it simply with the word "God." The following Sunday, Lencho arrives early to check his mail and shows absolutely no surprise upon seeing the money, such is his confidence. However, when he counts the cash, he becomes furious, convinced that God could not have made a mistake or denied his request. He immediately writes a second letter, drops it into the box, and leaves. When the postmaster eagerly opens it, he reads a shocking message: Lencho thanks God for the money but requests the remaining thirty pesos, strongly advising God not to send it through the mail because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks who stole his money, creating a powerful irony where the helpers are mistaken for thieves.

qa.a: ​ Lencho hoped for a good harvest because his crop needed rain. He was confident that the rain would bring him a rich harvest and provide enough food and money for his family.

qa.q: Why did Lencho say the raindrops were like “new coins”?
qa.a: ​ Lencho compared the raindrops to “new coins” because he believed the rain would help his crops grow well. A good harvest would bring him money and make his family financially secure.

qa.q: How did the rain change? What happened to Lencho’s fields?
qa.a: ​ The rain suddenly changed into a severe hailstorm. The hailstones destroyed the entire crop, including the corn and flowers. Lencho’s fields were completely ruined.

qa.q: What were Lencho’s feelings when the hail stopped?
qa.a: ​ Lencho was extremely sad and worried after the hailstorm. He knew that his entire crop had been destroyed and that his family would have nothing to eat. He felt that only God could help them now.

qa.q: Who or what did Lencho have faith in? What did he do?
qa.a: ​ Lencho had complete faith in God. After his crop was destroyed, he wrote a letter to God asking for one hundred pesos so that he could sow his field again and support his family.
​ The postmaster read Lencho’s letter to God. He was deeply impressed by Lencho’s strong faith and decided to help him.

qa.q: What did the postmaster do then?
qa.a: ​ The postmaster collected money from his employees and friends and contributed part of his own salary. He put the money in an envelope and sent it to Lencho in the name of God.

qa.q: Was Lencho surprised to find a letter for him with money in it?
qa.a: ​ No, Lencho was not surprised because he had complete faith in God. He believed that God had sent him the money in response to his letter.

qa.q: Who does Lencho have complete faith in? Which sentences in the story tell you this?
qa.a: ​ Lencho has complete faith in God. He believes that God sees everything and knows what he needs. Even after receiving less money than he had requested, he does not doubt God and believes that God must have sent the full amount.

qa.q: Why does the postmaster send money to Lencho? Why does he sign the letter “God”?
qa.a: ​ The postmaster sends money to Lencho because he is moved by Lencho’s strong faith in God. He does not want Lencho to lose his faith, so he collects money and sends it to him. He signs the letter “God” to make Lencho believe that God has answered his prayer.

qa.q: Did Lencho try to find out who had sent the money to him? Why/Why not?
qa.a: ​ No, Lencho did not try to find out who had sent the money. He had complete faith that God had sent it to him. He believed that God could never make a mistake.

qa.q: Who does Lencho think has taken the rest of the money? What is the irony in the situation?
qa.a: ​ Lencho thinks that the post office employees have taken the remaining money. The irony is that the postmaster and his employees were actually the people who collected and sent the money to him. Lencho’s complete faith in God makes him wrongly suspect the very people who helped him.

qa.q: Are there people like Lencho in the real world? What kind of attitude do they have towards others?
qa.a: ​ Yes, there are people who have strong faith like Lencho. They may be innocent and completely trusting, but sometimes they can misunderstand the actions of others. Such people may judge others based on their own beliefs without knowing the truth.
